statement: In 12 adults with moderate to severe major depressive disorder, mostly recurrent (one open-label proof-of-principle study in Norway, with no comparison group), two MDMA sessions about a month apart within a psychotherapy programme of about eleven sessions were followed, about 8 weeks after the second session, by a fall in clinician-rated depression (MADRS, scale 0 to 60: from 29.6 to 10.3, as corrected in a corrigendum; change −19.3, 95% CI −14.9 to −23.7), with 9 of 12 meeting both response and remission thresholds; functional impairment also fell. There were no serious adverse events, but worsening suicidal ideation was recorded as an adverse event in 4 to 6 of the 12 (the paper gives both figures) and 2 received benzodiazepines and zopiclone after dosing. The raters were not blind, almost all participants were self-referred, entry required a high score, and there was no control group, so the fall cannot be attributed to MDMA; the 7-month follow-up was not read. A network meta-analysis of randomized trials reporting depressive symptoms, whose MDMA trials enrolled mostly people with PTSD rather than depression, found a larger reduction with high-dose MDMA-assisted therapy than in the placebo arms of psychedelic trials (5.3 points on the HAMD-17, 95% credible interval 2.26 to 8.32), but could not show a difference from the placebo arms of antidepressant trials (1.5 points, −2.79 to 5.78, an indirect comparison; Hsu et al., 2024). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small study in Norway, 12 adults with depression had two MDMA sessions with talking therapy. About two months later, depression scores had dropped a lot, and 9 of the 12 were much better. But there was no group without MDMA, and the people rating depression knew everyone had taken it.
population: Adults with DSM-5 major depressive disorder (single or recurrent, without psychotic features; current episode 12 weeks to 2 years) and a MADRS of 20 or more; excluded: psychotic disorders, mania, personality disorders, eating disorders with purging, substance use disorders, serious suicide risk and cardiovascular risk; psychotropic medicines tapered
exposure: MDMA in two open-label day-long sessions about 4 weeks apart within MDMA-assisted therapy (three preparatory and six integration sessions)
outcome: Change in MADRS from baseline to about 8 weeks after the second session (primary); Sheehan Disability Scale; response and remission; adverse events
magnitude: MADRS 29.6 (SD 4.9) at baseline and 10.3 (8.3) at the outcome visit (corrigendum; first printed as 9.7, SD 10.0); change −19.3 (SD 8.3), bootstrap 95% CI −14.9 to −23.7, P < 0.001; responders (fall of 50% or more) 9 of 12 and remitters (MADRS 12 or less) 9 of 12; SDS 21.3 to 9.7, change −11.7 (95% CI −7.6 to −15.8). Adverse events: 46 in 10 of 12 participants (15 moderate, 31 mild), none serious; worsening intensity of suicidal ideation in 6 participants (12 events) by the Results, suicidal ideation in 33.3% by the Discussion; benzodiazepines and zopiclone for 2 participants within 2 days after dosing.

evidence.locator: Results › Primary outcome, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (MADRS row)
evidence.extracted: MADRS 29.6 (4.9) at baseline; mean change −19.3 (SD 8.3) to the outcome visit about 2 months after the second MDMA session; bootstrap 95% CI −14.9 to −23.7; z = −3.06, P < 0.001; among the 9 without comorbid PTSD, change −18.1 (8.8).

evidence.locator: Corrigendum text, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; corrected Table 2 (MADRS row)
evidence.extracted: One participant's post-treatment MADRS was wrong; corrected outcome mean 10.3 (SD 8.3) instead of 9.7 (10.0); change −19.3 (−14.9 to −23.7) unchanged; responder and remitter counts unaffected.

evidence.locator: Results › Exploratory analysis, 1st paragraph; Results › Secondary outcome, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Responders (MADRS fall of 50% or more) 9 of 12 and remitters (MADRS 12 or less) 9 of 12; SDS 21.3 (6.1) to 9.7 (9.2), change −11.7 (SD 7.6), 95% CI −7.6 to −15.8, P = 0.001.

46 adverse events in 10 of 12 participants (15 moderate, 31 mild), none serious, no discontinuations; most common headache, increased suicidal ideation and jaw muscle tightness; 2 participants received benzodiazepines and zopiclone within 2 days after dosing; no serious suicidal ideation or behaviour, but 6 participants (12 events) had a worsening in the intensity of suicidal ideation.

The authors give suicidal ideation as 33.3% when comparing with MAPP1; they state that without a control group the response cannot be attributed to the treatment rather than expectancy or natural fluctuation, that MADRS raters were neither completely independent nor blinded, and that adverse events reported to the therapy team may have been under-reported.

evidence.locator: Fig. 1 (CONSORT diagram, image); Results › Feasibility, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: 15 enrolled, 3 stopped before dosing, 12 dosed and analysed with none lost afterwards; 11 of 12 self-referred and 1 referred by a study therapist.

evidence.locator: EU Clinical Trials Register, trial 2021-000805-26 (NO) › E.2 Objectives; E.5 End points; record dates
evidence.extracted: Record first entered 4 August 2021, before recruitment (January 2023); open-label phase 2 feasibility study; main objective the mean change in MADRS (10 items, each rated 0 to 6) from baseline to about 12 weeks; registered secondary endpoint a subjective-effects scale, which the article does not report.

evidence.locator: Fig. 2, upper panel (values printed in the figure image)
evidence.extracted: Against the placebo arms of psychedelic trials: high-dose MDMA 5.32 HAMD-17 points (95% CrI 2.26 to 8.32), SMD 0.42; low-dose 4.92 (−0.26 to 9.94); extremely low dose 2.11 (−1.63 to 5.71).

evidence.locator: Fig. 2, middle and lower panels (values printed in the figure image); Results › Network meta-analysis, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Against the placebo arms of escitalopram trials: high-dose MDMA 1.53 (−2.79 to 5.78), SMD 0.08; against extremely low-dose psilocybin 1.36 (−3.08 to 5.84); the placebo arms of antidepressant trials did better than those of psychedelic trials (3.79, 0.77 to 6.80); against antidepressant-trial placebo only high-dose psilocybin and escitalopram had intervals excluding zero.

evidence.locator: Results › Network meta-analysis, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Data synthesis, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: High-dose psilocybin against high-dose MDMA 4.98 (1.23 to 8.67), SMD 0.32; the review judged clinical relevance against a minimal important difference of 3 HAMD-17 points.

evidence.locator: Results › Network meta-analysis, 1st paragraph; Methods › Data sources and searches; Discussion › Strengths and limitations of this study, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Searched from database inception to 12 October 2023; psychedelics were compared with the placebo arms of psychedelic trials and escitalopram with those of antidepressant trials, the two parts joined by one head-to-head psilocybin-escitalopram trial; participants in the MDMA trials were predominantly diagnosed with PTSD, those in the escitalopram trials with major depressive disorder; only acute effects were extracted.

evidence.locator: Results › All cause discontinuation and severe adverse event; Discussion › Comparison with other studies, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: No intervention had more all-cause discontinuation or severe adverse events than psychedelic-trial placebo; in the MDMA trials participants guessed their arm correctly in about 60% to 90% of cases.

risk_of_bias.note: Critical: no comparison; unblinded raters; regression to the mean.

grade.reasoning: One single-arm open-label study of 12 people: non-randomized, starts low. Risk of bias two levels (ROBINS-I critical): no comparison group; about eleven psychotherapy sessions, themselves an effective treatment for depression; entry required a MADRS of 20 or more, inviting regression to the mean; self-referred participants with probably high expectations; raters not blind. Imprecision one level: 12 participants. Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to this population and endpoint. The relation is 'insufficient evidence': the design cannot show whether MDMA changes depression, and the statement describes what was observed.

verification.flag_note: The seven-month follow-up of the same 12 participants (Kvam et al., 2026, J Psychiatr Res, doi 10.1016/j.jpsychires.2025.11.030) and the published commentary and reply (Br J Psychiatry 2026) have not been read; they should be read before this claim is shown.
